case_studies.title: CAVA: Canonical Action Verification and Attestation for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems
case_studies.abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly act through heterogeneous runtimes: local coding hooks, SDK tools, browser automation, managed-agent traces, API gateways, and workflow engines. A single operational act such as publishing code, changing identity state, moving money, or exporting data may therefore be represented by many incompatible runtime records. This makes a basic governance question difficult to answer: what action was actually approved, what evidence binds the approval to execution, and can an independent verifier reproduce the same action identity later? This paper presents Canonical Act
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of verifying actions in artificial intelligence systems that run on different platforms, by building a system called CAVA that can standardize and check these actions. The result is a way to ensure that AI systems are doing what they're supposed to do, and that their actions can be independently verified. This is relevant to IT teams managing AI and automation systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI or automation systems, here is what to do: review your current governance processes, identify potential gaps in action verification, and consider implementing a standardized system like CAVA to ensure accountability and transparency. This flags a risk: if your org uses multiple runtime environments for AI, check your logging and auditing processes immediately to ensure they can verify actions across platforms. If you only manage traditional infrastructure, this research is not directly applicable to your work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a method for governance of agentic AI systems, which is relevant to IT engineers working with large-scale AI deployments. It presents a novel approach for Canonical Action Verification and Attestation, which could lead to more reliable and secure AI system governance. However, its value in the real world might be limited to large enterprises and its deployment timeframe is uncertain. IT engineers might be interested in forwarding this to colleagues working on agentic systems or with governance of AI systems, so the novelty score is relatively high.

case_studies.title: Copy-on-Write Scoring: Application-Specific Agent Evaluations
case_studies.abstract: Trustworthy deployment of LLM-based agents in software systems requires evaluating how they perform on application-specific workflows, with enough granularity to localize where they succeed and fail. Yet existing agent evaluation mechanisms are limited: benchmarks have low construct validity for application-specific workflows and environments, and replica evaluation environments are expensive and prone to drift. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating the performance of Large Language Model (LLM) agents in specific software workflows. The authors built a framework called Copy-on-Write Scoring, which evaluates agent operations within application environments. The result is a more accurate assessment of agent performance, localized to specific workflows and environments.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on evaluating LLM agent performance within software applications.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper discusses novel method for evaluating LLM-based agents in application-specific workflows. IT relevance because it deals with LLM APIs and could have implications for DevOps automation. Value within 90 days as it could inform the development of more accurate and cost-effective agent evaluation methods. Low IT relevance signal, but paper has sufficient novelty and value to push score above 40.

case_studies.title: When Words Are Safe But Actions Kill: Probing Physical Danger Beyond Text Safety in Hidden-State Risk Space
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as high-level planners for embodied agents, where linguistically benign instructions can become unsafe once grounded in the physical world. We study whether this physically grounded danger is the same safety problem as ordinary text-level content danger. Through hidden-state direction analysis and random-split null tests, we show that content danger (CD) and physical danger (PD) form separable signals in LLM representations across Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B/32B, Phi-3.5 and SmolLM2. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of language models producing physically dangerous actions despite having safe text instructions. The researchers built a system called PRISM to separate text-level safety from physical danger. The result shows that text safety and physical safety are separate signals in language models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the safety of language models in physical environments, rather than cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: 15 - reveals something about large language model safety with physical implications. IT Relevance: 10 - directly affects how IT engineers deploy LLMs with potential agentic systems. Value: 15 - proposes a new risk detection method (PRISM) which could be implemented within 90 days in high-stakes environments.

case_studies.title: ToolAlignBench: Investigating Alignment Conflicts in Tool-Calling Enabled LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Safety alignment in LLMs aims to align models with human values, but which values take precedence when they conflict? We investigate this question in the context of tool-calling LLM agents deployed in regulated industries, where agents processing confidential documents may encounter content that triggers safety-trained values (e.g., public welfare) that conflict with deployment-context instructions (e.g., internal logging). To empirically verify this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of 128 scenarios across 16 domains. We find that safety-aligned open-source models override their deployment ins
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of alignment conflicts in large language models (LLMs) by investigating how they handle conflicting values. The researchers built a benchmark of 128 scenarios to test this phenomenon. The result shows that safety-aligned models can override their deployment instructions in certain situations.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the development and testing of LLMs rather than their deployment or management in cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty (2): Reveals surprising conflicts in safety-aligned LLMs. IT Relevance (18): Directly affects how IT engineers work with LLMs in regulated industries. Value (35): IT engineers and consultants can use this to inform risk management and propose services to clients within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?
case_studies.abstract: AI benchmarks increasingly leverage item-level statistical models, particularly item response theory (IRT), to estimate model capabilities, rank systems, select informative examples, and diagnose benchmark quality. However, AI benchmark data often departs from the data regime of human testing, for which standard IRT estimation tools were originally developed: benchmarks typically involve fewer evaluated models, far more items, and capability distributions that may be skewed, clustered, or multimodal. We examine how these regime mismatches challenge the reliability of IRT modeling for AI evalua
case_studies.summary: This research examines the reliability of item response theory for evaluating AI models, finding that current methods may not be suitable due to differences in data regimes. The authors investigated how AI benchmark data challenges the reliability of standard IRT estimation tools. The result highlights potential issues with current AI evaluation methods.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty due to unexpected use of IRT in AI. Relevance is low as it affects AI benchmarks but not directly how IT engineers work. Value within 90 days is moderate, as IT engineers may be concerned about AI benchmark reliability.

case_studies.title: Learning Safe Agent Behaviour from Human Preferences and Justifications via World Models
case_studies.abstract: We address the problem of safely training an agent policy and deploying a good and safe policy, in settings where the environment dynamics are unknown and no suitable reward function is available. In the context of safety-critical environments, we consider traditional reinforcement learning impractical and resort to the resource of human input. We introduce DROPJ, a human-centred method for both safe training and deployment. We first learn a world model (a learned simulator) from a dataset of prior real-world trajectories. A human then plays the game in this learned simulator to extract severa
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of safely training an agent policy in unknown environments with no suitable reward function by introducing a human-centred method called DROPJ. The researchers built a world model from prior real-world trajectories and used human input to extract safe training data. The result is a safer deployment of agent policies in safety-critical environments.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on training agent policies in safety-critical environments rather than managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper has moderate novelty in introducing DROPJ, a human-centred method for safe agent training and deployment. IT relevance is moderate as it deals with safe agent behaviour but is quite theoretical without direct practical applications. However, value in 90 days is low as it would require significant resources to implement DROPJ and deploy it safely.

case_studies.title: Rubrics on Trial: Evolving Rubrics from a Single Query via Synthetic Pairwise Evidence
case_studies.abstract: Rubrics provide structured, fine-grained signals for training and evaluating large language models (LLMs). Yet reliable query-specific rubrics are difficult to construct. Existing approaches often derive supervision from human-written rubrics, preference data, or sampled responses. Direct query-to-rubric generation avoids these resources, but provides no explicit check that a plausible rubric is useful. Such a rubric may fail to distinguish answer quality, reward an optional style, or penalize a valid alternative strategy. We introduce Rubrics on Trial, a query-only framework that evolves a ru
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of creating reliable query-specific rubrics for training large language models. The authors built a framework called Rubrics on Trial that generates rubrics from a single query. The result is a more effective way to evaluate and train language models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty in IT-Relevance due to discussion of LLMs and rubrics. Medium relevance as it focuses on query-specific rubrics which can be useful in practical applications. Value 90 days as the paper proposes a solution to the query-to-rubric problem which can be useful for practical LLM deployment. Low monetisation potential as the topic doesn't lend itself to direct commercial application.

case_studies.title: SAFETY SENTRY: Context-Aware Human Intervention via EXECUTE-ASK-REFUSE Routing
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents act on real-world environments through tool calls, and a single misjudged action can cause irreversible harm. The standard safeguard is a guard model that labels each proposed action as safe or unsafe, but this binary view conflates two distinct decisions: whether the action is harmful in itself, and whether it is appropriate given the user's context. It also operates at the granularity of action categories rather than individual instances, producing routine interruptions that erode autonomy and train users to wave through the most consequential alerts. We reframe the problem as a p
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of LLM agents causing harm in real-world environments due to misjudged actions, by building a context-aware human intervention system, resulting in more informed and autonomous decision-making. The system, called SAFETY SENTRY, routes actions through an execute-ask-refuse process, considering user context and individual action instances. This improves the safety and usability of LLM-powered systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM-powered systems, here is what to do: review your current safeguard measures, consider integrating a context-aware intervention system like SAFETY SENTRY, and assess the potential impact on your system's autonomy and user experience. This flags a risk: if your org uses LLM agents to interact with real-world environments, check your current guard models for potential gaps in context-aware decision-making immediately. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to those working with LLM-powered systems.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper focuses on LLM safety and context-aware human intervention, which affects IT engineers who deploy and manage such systems. However, the deployment angle is limited and the value within 90 days is low. Also, there's no direct mention of IT infrastructure, SaaS tooling or automation which scores low on IT_RELEVANCE and VALUE_90_DAYS.

case_studies.title: On-Policy Delta Distillation
case_studies.abstract: On-policy distillation is an alternative post-training method in reinforcement learning that alleviates the constraints imposed by reward models by providing token-level supervision from a teacher model. Although on-policy distillation has been studied and applied across various settings, its fundamental design remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a new distillation reward, termed the delta signal, instead of directly imitating the teacher's output distribution. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of improving reinforcement learning models by introducing a new distillation reward called the delta signal, which is used to train a model by comparing the difference between a teacher model and its base model. The authors built a new method called On-Policy Delta Distillation, which provides token-level supervision from a teacher model. The result is a more effective way to train reinforcement learning models without relying on reward models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it relates to reinforcement learning models and training methods, which are typically handled by data science or machine learning teams.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper introduces a new technique in reinforcement learning, but relevance to IT infrastructure or deployment is limited. The delta signal may have implications in some AI models but is too early for real-world impact or monetization.
